name: Cantharidin solution
lead: Cantharidin is a blistering agent made by blister beetles that dermatologists apply to skin to remove molluscum contagiosum bumps and warts.[1][2] It helps looks by clearing visible lesions, and the blister-and-lift approach is reported to heal without scarring.[1] A prescription topical, Ycanth (VP-102), was approved by the FDA in July 2023 for molluscum contagiosum.[1]

Cantharidin was first isolated in 1810 by Pierre Robiquet from the beetles once sold as 'Spanish fly'.[1] Its use against warts was studied by 1958.[1] Phase 3 trials of VP-102 in molluscum enrolled over 500 people, and phase 2 trials examined common and genital warts.[3][4][2]

chain: Cantharidin applied to lesions by a clinician
Blister forms and lifts the lesion
angle.text: A clinician paints the solution on molluscum bumps or warts, a blister forms and the lesion lifts away, typically healing without scarring. People seek it to clear visible bumps cosmetically and avoid scraping or freezing.

paras: Approved use is treatment of molluscum contagiosum in patients aged 2 and older.[1] Dilute solutions have also been used for common warts, and VP-102 has been tested on genital warts.[1][6] Molluscum lesions often clear by themselves in six to twelve months, and people who treat them do so for cosmetic reasons or to prevent spread.[7]

Two phase 3 randomized trials (about 262 and 266 participants) tested cantharidin application in molluscum, and the FDA approval was based on two double-blind placebo-controlled trials.[1][3][4] A phase 2 trial of 56 patients examined cantharidin with occlusion on common warts, and a 105-patient placebo-controlled phase 2 study tested VP-102 on external genital warts.[2][6] Cantharidin-induced blisters are also used as a research model of skin inflammation.[8]

Topical effects include pain and blistering, and severe chemical burns can occur; lesions heal without scarring per the encyclopedia account.[1][7] Swallowing cantharidin can cause serious gastrointestinal and kidney damage and is fatal at high doses.[1]

Cantharides preparations were used from antiquity as aphrodisiacs and irritants, and Robiquet isolated the pure compound in 1810.[1] Verrica's Ycanth became the first FDA-approved molluscum treatment in 2023.[1]

timeline.event: Study of cantharidin for warts published.[1]

card.summary: A clinician-applied blistering solution that lifts off molluscum bumps and warts for clearer skin.
card.note: Can cause blisters and chemical burns; toxic if swallowed.

quick.overview:
Cantharidin is a blistering compound from blister beetles. Dermatologists apply it to molluscum bumps and warts so a blister lifts the lesion away.

The FDA approved the Ycanth formulation for molluscum in July 2023.
quick.mechanism: It causes a controlled blister in the skin layer holding the lesion; the blister heals and the lesion goes with it, reportedly without scarring.
quick.risks: Pain, blisters and chemical burns can occur on skin. Swallowing it can cause serious kidney and gut damage. It is prescription and clinician-applied.
